content: The Expanded Very Large Array needs an operations system for configuring and monitoring its radio-astronomy correlator and processing the resulting data stream in real time. Scientists and engineers should be able to inspect system health and observational data, while the software assembles and transforms correlator output into usable results for downstream storage and analysis. The system should identify faults and recover automatically where practical.

At a high level, the operators need to set up the correlator for the planned observation, watch it continuously while the array is running, and make sure the output is being transformed into usable data without gaps or corruption. During the run, the system has to show whether the correlator and the downstream processing chain are healthy, and it should flag anything that looks like a fault or performance issue quickly enough for someone to act on it.
Once the observation starts, the correlator output needs to be ingested in real time, checked, and assembled into the right form for storage and later analysis. If something fails, we’d want the system to recover automatically when it can, or at least isolate the problem and preserve as much good data as possible. The overall mission is basically to keep the observing session moving smoothly while turning raw correlator data into reliable scientific results.

The main rule is that changes have to be coordinated with the observing schedule and the current state of the array, because we can’t just reconfigure the correlator arbitrarily in the middle of a science run. In practice, we’d expect some changes to be allowed only at safe points, and others to be blocked if they would disrupt data integrity or make the current scan unusable. If the conditions aren’t met, the pipeline should refuse the change, keep processing whatever valid data it can, and clearly report why the request was rejected or deferred.
If a pause or restart is needed because of a fault, the system should do that in a controlled way so we don’t lose track of what data is good and what isn’t. I’d also want the pipeline to mark any affected interval so downstream users know there was an interruption or configuration change.

If a change isn’t safe, the system should hold it pending or reject it outright depending on whether it can be applied later without breaking the observation. It should not force a risky change through, because data quality and schedule compliance matter more than convenience in that moment. The operator needs a clear explanation of what blocked it and whether it can be retried at the next safe boundary.
For the data stream, it should continue processing only the valid portion and clearly separate any interval affected by the failed request or interruption. I’d want that segment flagged in a way that downstream users can recognize it as incomplete, suspect, or unusable, rather than silently blending it into normal results.

We’d want to protect operational status, configuration settings, fault logs, and the real-time observational products coming off the correlator, especially anything that could reveal scheduling details or system weaknesses. Some of that isn’t highly sensitive in a security sense, but it is operationally important, so access should still be limited to people who need it for their job. In particular, raw and near-real-time data should not be broadly shared outside the operations and science support groups without approval.
Practically, I’d expect role-based access, basic auditability, and controlled export of stored data. If something is being used for troubleshooting or collaboration, it should be shared in a way that avoids exposing unnecessary internal details or unreleased observing information.

It needs to be supportable by the operations staff on duty, with enough visibility to diagnose problems quickly and enough automation to reduce routine intervention. Over time, I’d expect the system to be maintained as the correlator and processing chain evolve, so configuration logic, monitoring thresholds, and recovery behavior may need updates without disrupting observing too much. We’d also want it to be easy to add new health checks, data products, and interfaces as the observatory’s needs change.
The important thing is that changes remain controlled and testable, because this is a live operations environment. So the system should be built and maintained in a way that lets us improve it incrementally while preserving reliability and traceability.

For the initial release, I’d want the core configuration, monitoring, real-time ingest, basic fault detection, and safe recovery behavior in place, because those are the things needed to run observations day to day. We also need the essential operator displays and status reporting so staff can tell quickly whether the correlator and processing chain are healthy. If there’s one priority, it’s making sure the system can support live operations reliably.
Things like richer analytics, more advanced visualization, broader integrations, or specialized reports can probably wait for later phases. I’d rather have a smaller system that is solid and trusted than a larger one that does too much before it’s operationally stable.

If the change can be made without altering the meaning or continuity of the current scan, then it can be applied immediately. If it would affect calibration, data formatting, or any live processing state in a way that could confuse downstream users, it should be deferred until a safe boundary like the end of the scan or a planned pause. And if the change would clearly compromise the current observation or violate the observing plan, it should be rejected.
The system should use the current observing state, the type of requested change, and any known dependency on the processing pipeline to make that call. When it defers or rejects a request, it needs to say why in operational terms, not just return a generic error.

The guiding rule should be whether the unaffected portion still has clear scientific meaning and can be separated cleanly from the disrupted part. If the valid segment is trustworthy on its own, the system should continue from that point and mark the bad interval so downstream users know exactly where the break occurred. If the disruption contaminates the whole product or makes the boundary ambiguous, then it should stop that product rather than risk handing out something misleading.
In other words, preserve usable data when it can be isolated, but don’t try to salvage a stream if doing so would blur the line between good and bad information. The system should make that decision conservatively.

Approval should come from someone with operational authority for the data set, usually based on role and the purpose of the export. Routine internal use can be lighter weight, but anything leaving the observatory or involving near-real-time products should be controlled more carefully and may need explicit approval. We’d want the system to enforce that only authorized staff can request or release exports.
As for content, it should allow export of the needed data product but strip or restrict sensitive operational details when appropriate, like internal host information, security-relevant diagnostics, or unreleased observing information. If the data is still near-real-time, I’d expect additional restrictions so it isn’t broadly redistributed until it’s cleared for that purpose.

In day-to-day use, people usually mean things like configuring the correlator, starting or stopping a scan, watching the data stream, checking health and alarms, and confirming that the output is being assembled correctly for storage. The important work steps are usually setup, live monitoring, reacting to faults, and handing data off cleanly to the next processing or archive stage. Those are the terms everyone needs to understand in the same way for operations to go smoothly.
The biggest room for different interpretations is usually around words like “good data,” “safe to change,” or “recovered,” because engineers and scientists may judge those differently. We’d need the system to use those terms consistently and make the current state explicit so nobody has to guess what it means in a given situation.

It should clearly distinguish the raw correlator stream, any intermediate processed product, and the final stored science output. At a glance, staff should be able to tell the observation, time range, processing stage, and whether the product is provisional, validated, or affected by a fault. That way nobody confuses something meant for quick operational use with something ready for archive or analysis.
I’d also want the labels to be consistent across displays, logs, and exported files, so the same product is recognized everywhere. If there are any local conventions already in use, the system should follow those rather than inventing a brand-new naming scheme.

Yes, I’d define the boundaries now even if we don’t build them yet. Rich analytics and specialized reports should only become available once the underlying data product is validated and no longer provisional, and advanced visualization should be limited if the stream is still live, unstable, or partially recovered. Broader integrations should wait until we’ve proven the core operational workflow and can control what external systems can see.
I’d also say anything that could influence active observing decisions should be withheld unless it’s based on trusted, current state. So later-phase features are fine, but they should respect the same rules about data quality, operational safety, and release status from the start.

The screen should make the stage obvious in the product name itself, not just in a separate status field. I’d expect terms like raw, processed, or archive-ready to be shown consistently, and the state should be called out right next to it with something like live, provisional, validated, or fault-affected. If a product changes state, that label needs to update immediately so staff don’t rely on stale assumptions.
Color or icon cues can help, but they shouldn’t be the only signal. The text should still be clear enough that someone can tell at a glance whether they’re looking at something suitable for operations, something tentative, or something that should not be used without caution.

Yes, any locally established observation IDs, scan numbers, project codes, and processing-stage names should be preserved exactly, because people already use those to cross-check systems. If there are abbreviations in common use, I’d keep them as-is on the operational screens and in logs, as long as they remain unambiguous. The main acceptable difference is presentation: displays can be friendlier or more compact, while exported files should be more explicit and machine-consistent.
If we need to add anything new, I’d keep it as a supplemental label rather than renaming the existing one. That avoids breaking the habits and tools staff already rely on.

Normal operations need to handle a continuous high-rate stream without gaps, because the correlator output is effectively always on whenever we’re observing. I don’t have an exact number for the data rate, but it is enough that the system has to process and monitor in real time rather than in batches. During busy periods, the main change is not necessarily a different stream type, but more simultaneous observations, more operator attention, and less tolerance for delay or backpressure.
What matters most is that the system keeps up consistently and makes overload visible before it affects the observation. If there are peak rates or seasonal busy windows, I’d need to check those with the operations team.

Yes, we should assume future observing modes could be substantially more demanding than what we run today. New modes may increase channel count, time resolution, or the number of simultaneous outputs, which would all raise the processing and monitoring load even if the observing cadence feels similar. So the boundary condition I’d want is that the core operations path should have headroom for growth, not just fit today’s steady state.
I don’t know the exact future numbers yet, but I’d treat a step change in data volume as likely rather than exceptional. That means the design should avoid hard-coded limits where possible and make any scaling constraints very visible.

Live changes should be limited to things that restore service or reduce risk without changing the scientific meaning of the current observation, like restarting a failed component, rerouting around a dead path, or switching to a safe degraded mode. Anything that alters calibration, output interpretation, or the structure of the processing chain should be held for a controlled window, because we need to know exactly what effect it had on the data. If there’s any doubt about whether a change would affect the observation, I’d rather it be deferred.
We also need a clear line on what counts as recovery versus reconfiguration. Recovery can happen automatically when practical, but major behavioral changes should require operator approval and probably a planned test or maintenance period.

I’d define the controlled-and-testable items now, at least at the category level, because those boundaries matter in live operations. Configuration logic, recovery behavior, health checks, and any interface that operators rely on should be treated as controlled, meaning changes need to be testable and reversible before they can affect production observing. Monitoring thresholds and data product definitions should also be controlled if changing them would alter alarms or the meaning of the output.
I’d leave the exact implementation details tentative for now, but not the rule that those areas are protected. That way we can still evolve the system, while making sure live operations stay predictable and safe.

Before anything is trusted in live observing, it should be proven in a staging or simulation environment that behaves closely enough to the real system. For a recovery action, I’d want evidence that it restores the service without corrupting the current data stream or hiding the underlying fault. For a configuration change or new health check, we need verification that it does what it claims, that alerts are accurate, and that it doesn’t create extra noise or operator confusion during an actual observing run.
If the exception has already disrupted the correlator or pipeline, then the first priority is validating the system is back in a known-good state before resuming normal output. I’d also want the change to be logged and traceable so we can review exactly what happened afterward.

Access should be limited to the people who actually need it for operations, engineering, or validation, and we should treat staging data with the same care as production wherever it contains sensitive operational details. If real observatory data or restricted metadata is used, then only approved users should be able to see it, and we should keep an audit trail of who accessed what and when. I’d also prefer that test environments use sanitized or representative data by default, with real sensitive data only when there’s a clear operational reason.
The practical rule is that validation should not become a back door into restricted information. So access control, logging, and role-based permissions need to be enforced consistently across staging and simulation.

Yes, I’d like to specify some minimum realism and approval conditions now. The staging or simulation should be close enough to the live correlator and pipeline that it exercises the same interfaces, timing expectations, and failure modes, otherwise the validation won’t mean much. For anything that affects recovery behavior, configuration, or health checks, I’d want an explicit sign-off from the operations side before it’s allowed into live observing.
The exact acceptance criteria can stay tentative for now, but the principle shouldn’t. We need a realistic test environment and a human approval gate for changes that can alter live behavior.

The exception should be allowed only when synthetic or anonymized data isn’t sufficient to validate the specific operational behavior we care about. In that case, we should keep only the minimum amount of real data needed for the test, and sanitize anything that isn’t essential to the validation goal. If a field isn’t required to prove the change works, it should be masked or removed.
I’d also want that exception to be explicitly approved and documented, so we can justify why real data was necessary. The default should always be sanitized data first, real data only as a limited exception.

It should record the person or service account, the time, the environment or dataset touched, the action taken, and the approval or ticket that authorized it. I’d also include enough detail to reconstruct the activity later, like whether data was viewed, copied, modified, or used in a test run, but not the sensitive contents themselves. The goal is traceability, not duplication of the data.
If we can keep the log at that level, it should satisfy accountability without exposing more operational information than necessary.

In general, I’d only allow a live-impacting change to proceed without operations sign-off if it is a fully automated, pre-approved safeguard action that has already been validated and is narrowly limited, like a routine self-recovery step with no change to observing intent. Anything that alters correlator configuration, data products, alert thresholds, or the interpretation of live health status should definitely require operations approval.
The boundary is whether the change can affect observing results or operator decisions in a way that isn’t completely predictable and reversible. If it can, then it needs sign-off.

A good practical rule is that if the change can alter live data quality, observing continuity, or what operators believe about system health, it stops for approval. Even if it is partially reversible, that’s still not enough if undoing it could leave gaps, change timestamps, or make the current observing state ambiguous. In other words, automation can act only when the action is bounded, fully understood, and safe to retry or roll back without affecting the observation.
If there’s any chance the change could influence the science stream or the operator’s decision-making, I’d treat it as requiring operations approval.

We’d want to see that the correlator has re-synchronized cleanly, the data path is flowing again without gaps or corruption, and the pipeline has restarted from a known checkpoint or otherwise recovered in a controlled way. I’d also want current health indicators to be green, the configuration to match the expected observing setup, and at least a short period of stable output after recovery before we declare it normal again. If there was a fault, the system should also show that it cleared the fault condition rather than just masking it.
For anything significant, I’d prefer a brief operator review of the recovery evidence before resuming full trust in the output.

The new approach needs to keep the observatory able to configure and monitor the correlator in real time, keep the data stream moving into usable products, and give scientists and engineers clear visibility into health and observing status. It also needs to support fault detection and practical automatic recovery, because downtime and manual intervention are expensive during live observing. On the business side, the big goal is continuity: the replacement has to preserve operations without forcing the team to relearn everything at once.
The biggest scope boundary is the observing workflow itself. We can improve the tooling and underlying implementation, but we should not change the meaning of core operational states, the approval responsibilities, or the basic way people trust live output unless there’s a very strong reason. If anything, the new system should fit into existing processes rather than redefine them.

Those later-phase features should only turn on once the core live path is stable, recovery behavior has been proven, and we’ve run them against real observing sessions without impacting the correlator or the primary pipeline. I’d want a clear operational gate for each one: analytics and reporting can come on first if they’re read-only and based on trusted output, while visualization and external integrations need extra caution if they could confuse operators or feed other systems with unverified status. Anything that could influence live observing decisions, trigger automation elsewhere, or present incomplete data as authoritative should stay off until the workflow is trusted end to end.
In practice, read-only features are acceptable earlier, but anything that writes back, automates decisions, or exposes operational status outside the control room should remain unavailable until the team is confident the data stream is stable and the semantics are settled.

They should come only from already trusted operational data, like finalized correlator output, stable health metrics, and non-sensitive session metadata, not from raw debug feeds or anything that could expose internal secrets or operator notes. Access should be limited to people who already have a legitimate operations or science need, and we should separate general reporting from anything that includes troubleshooting detail or performance anomalies. If a report could be used to infer live system weaknesses or still-changing observing conditions, I’d treat it as restricted and require approval to broaden access.
We’d also want approval boundaries around any dataset that crosses from simple summary information into records that could be operationally sensitive, like exact failure timelines, configuration deltas, or anything tied to a specific incident review.

A report can stay in the trusted-summary category if it only shows stable, aggregated information that has already been cleared as part of normal operations, like session status, uptime, and high-level performance trends. Once it starts showing fine-grained timestamps, raw error traces, fault sequences, configuration changes, or anything that helps reconstruct an active incident, it becomes troubleshooting detail and should be restricted. The practical line is whether the report is useful for routine oversight only, or whether it would help someone diagnose, replay, or exploit a live weakness.
If there’s any chance the report could reveal an unresolved anomaly or expose incident-sensitive records before they’ve been reviewed, I’d err on the side of restriction.

That should require explicit operations approval, not automatic publication. In practice I’d expect the system to flag the dataset as incident-sensitive, hold it from general access, and present it to the operations lead or incident owner for release approval. Only after they confirm it’s appropriate for review or wider sharing should it move out of the restricted state.
If we can, the approval should also record who approved it and for what purpose, so we have a clear audit trail.

Any change that can alter alarms or the meaning of output should go through a controlled change process with explicit approval from operations, and usually science or engineering sign-off if it affects interpretation. Before production use, it should be tested in a staging or shadow mode against real or representative data so we can confirm it doesn’t create false alarms, hide real ones, or change the reported products in an unexpected way. We’d also want a clear rollback path to the previous thresholds or definition, and the rollout should be gradual if possible rather than a hard switch.
If the change affects live observing confidence, it should not be allowed to auto-promote just because the software was deployed; someone needs to verify the results and release it into production use.

Staging or shadow testing is sufficient when the change is limited, the impact is easy to understand, and the results match the old behavior closely enough that we’re only adjusting sensitivity or presentation, not the underlying operational meaning. It also needs to run cleanly through a few real observing sessions without introducing false alarms, missed alarms, or confusion for the operators. If the change touches a critical threshold, a core derived product, or anything that would alter how we’d react during a live observation, then I’d want a longer trial and more review before it goes live.
I’d block it entirely if we can’t validate the new behavior against real conditions, if the old meaning would no longer be preserved, or if the risk of misleading operators is too high.

The rollout should be gradual, with the new behavior enabled for a small, controlled subset first, and only expanded after operators confirm it behaves as expected in real observing. During that period, both the old and new results should be observable enough to compare, so we can see whether alarms shift in a meaningful way or whether the output starts to confuse people. If we see a spike in false alarms, missed alarms, inconsistent outputs, or operator uncertainty, that should trigger an immediate rollback to the previous trusted behavior.
I’d also make rollback mandatory if the new definition changes how a live decision would be made and we can’t quickly explain or verify the difference.

Access to real observatory data in staging or simulation should be tightly limited to people directly involved in validating the system, and only for the minimum data needed. If the data includes restricted metadata or anything sensitive about live operations, I’d want approval from the operations lead or data owner before it’s used, not just a developer or tester making that call on their own. The access should be time-limited and scoped to the specific session or test purpose.
We should log who requested it, who approved it, what data was exposed, when it was used, and when access ended, so there’s a clear audit trail. If possible, the staging environment should use masked or reduced datasets by default, and real data should be the exception.

Even if a feature is read-only, I’d keep it disabled if the output is known to be incomplete, delayed, or still subject to correction from the live pipeline. Anything that could cause someone outside the control room to act on stale or partial information should stay off until we’re confident it’s safe to share. I’d also hold it back if the data contains sensitive operational context that hasn’t been cleared for that audience, even if nobody can modify it.
If there’s any doubt about whether the view could be mistaken for authoritative, that’s enough reason to delay it.

Staging access should start only when there’s a specific approved test or validation activity, and it should end automatically when that session is over or the window expires. If someone needs more time, they should request a renewal rather than just keeping access open, and that renewal should be approved again if the scope has changed. If they want to use the access for a different purpose, that should be treated as a new request, because the original approval shouldn’t cover an unrelated test.
We’d want the system to enforce that pretty strictly so staging doesn’t drift into general use.

A renewal can stay under the same approval if it’s the same test objective, the same people, the same dataset or environment scope, and we’re just needing more time to finish what was already approved. If the focus has shifted, if new data sources or permissions are needed, or if the work might affect a different system behavior than originally reviewed, that should trigger a fresh review. I’d also want a new review if the extension starts to look open-ended rather than tied to a specific validation task.
If it’s just a short overrun on the original session, same purpose and same controls, then a simple extension is fine.

We’d want the monitoring and output path to have enough headroom that a normal increase in load doesn’t push it right up against the limit during routine observing. Practically, that means it should still stay stable and responsive with the expected next step up in channel count or output volume, plus a margin for short spikes and processing overhead. If supporting the new mode would require running so close to capacity that delays, dropped samples, or stale alarms become likely, then the current design is too small for safe real-time use.
If the growth forces major redesign of buffering, processing, or display/update timing just to keep up, I’d treat that as beyond what we should absorb casually and flag it for a broader architecture review.

We should leave the exact growth number open for now unless someone on the operations or correlator side can give us a firm forecast. What I would want captured is that the design must accommodate reasonable near-term expansion without a full rewrite, but I’m not comfortable inventing a percentage or factor without checking the actual road map. If needed, we can come back and set a concrete margin once the observing plans are clearer.

If the change can be handled by tuning thresholds, adding a parser, widening a buffer, or introducing another check without changing the basic data flow, that feels like an incremental extension. Once the observatory evolution starts affecting timing guarantees, ordering, fault handling, or the way operators interpret the data, I’d treat it as a redesign issue rather than a simple configuration change. Anything that could compromise real-time behavior or make the monitoring less trustworthy should go through a more formal review before we implement it.

Yes, definitely. If the system is in a provisional, recovering, or unstable state, I’d limit anything that could be mistaken for final science-quality output or authoritative health status. In those cases, it’s better to show clearly that the data are partial or degraded, and keep higher-trust presentation or external output withheld until the system is back in a stable final state.

A good boundary is whether the change preserves the current operational model or whether it changes how people actually run or trust the system. If it introduces a new workflow, changes the meaning of alarms or displayed results, or alters fault recovery in a way operators must learn differently, that should go through formal review. If it just adds another supported case inside the existing model, then it can probably stay incremental.

We should tighten access whenever the data reveals live operational status, fault conditions, operator activity, or anything that could be used to infer how the array is being run in real time. I’d also treat anything tied to internal troubleshooting, recovery actions, or unfinished calibrations as restricted until it’s cleared for broader use. If the data is just routine summarized status with no operational sensitivity, then it can be shared more normally.

Yes, if the data includes live control commands, fault logs, recovery actions, or operator-identifying activity, that should automatically be treated as restricted. I’d also restrict access by role so that routine observers can see summarized status, but only operations, engineering, or other authorized staff can see the more detailed real-time behavior. The exact role names and thresholds would need to match our site policy, but the principle is that anything exposing active control or troubleshooting should not be broadly visible.

During an incident or a formal drill, a routine observer could be allowed to see more than the usual summary if that helps them understand what is happening without disturbing operations. Even then, I’d still hide anything that exposes command-level control, operator identities, or detailed recovery steps that could be misused or cause confusion. They can know the system is degraded and what broad subsystem is affected, but not the exact actions being taken in real time.

I’d treat it as unsafe once the system can no longer absorb normal spikes without missing deadlines, because then the monitoring and output stop being trustworthy in real time. If a new mode or higher channel count pushes us so close to saturation that alarms lag, samples get dropped, or recovery can’t keep up, that has crossed the limit. At that point we need either more capacity or a redesign of the processing path rather than just accepting the extra load.

It should be tied to sustained latency and to whether recovery is falling behind, not just average throughput. If delays stay above the acceptable window long enough that the displayed state or output is no longer current, or if repeated spikes keep pushing the system further behind, then the real-time path is no longer acceptable for normal use. Even if the average rate looks fine, stale alarms or outputs are a hard stop for us.
